researchLines.title: Dialectic and Ignorance as Self-Deception
researchLines.shortDescription: A study of Socratic examination as a process of rational self-clarification against the illusion of knowledge.
researchLines.extendedDescription: Against purely refutative or eristic readings, this line approaches Socratic aporia not as a mere logical dead end but as the dialectical engine that dismantles the self-concealing structure of error and reveals the subject's fundamental self-deception.
philosophicalQuestions: Why does moral and epistemic error tend to protect itself?
How can the perplexity induced by dialogue open up space for genuine learning?
In what way does dialogical examination transform the interlocutor's background beliefs?

researchLines.title: Dialectic and Affectivity
researchLines.shortDescription: An analysis of the constitutive role of emotions such as perplexity, shame, wonder, and friendship.
researchLines.extendedDescription: Socratic rationality does not operate in an impassive vacuum. We investigate how affects (the blush of dialectical shame, wonder, perplexity, pedagogical eros, and philia) are intrinsic conditions for dialectical reasoning to generate existential commitment and a change of life.
philosophicalQuestions: Is shame a morally indispensable emotion in Socratic refutation?
What role does intellectual friendship play in shared dialectical perseverance?
How does Socrates overcome the modern dichotomy between emotion and pure reason?

researchLines.title: Dialectic and Transmission (Pedagogical and Political)
researchLines.shortDescription: The pedagogical and political dimensions of Socratic paideia and its contemporary reception.
researchLines.extendedDescription: We examine Socratic paideia as a public, communal, and political proposal, analyzing how critical examination is transmitted from person to person and how it has been reactivated in ancient philosophy (Hellenism, Stoicism, Cynicism) and in contemporary philosophy (both analytic and continental, from Foucault and Hadot to McDowell and Callard).
philosophicalQuestions: How does Socrates reconcile private, individual questioning with the well-being of the polis?
In what sense does Philosophy as a Way of Life (PWL) require rigorous logic and not merely aseptic practices?
What lessons does Socratic practice offer for the deliberative challenges of contemporary democracies?

readingList.author: Agnes Callard
readingList.title: Open Socrates
readingList.notes: An examination of the Socratic figure as a model of radical disagreement and dialogical transformation in the present.

readingList.author: D. Futter
readingList.title: Socrates' Search for Wisdom. An Exegetical Theory
readingList.notes: An analytic and textual reconstruction of the Socratic method of inquiry in the early Platonic dialogues.

readingList.author: Pierre Hadot
readingList.title: What Is Ancient Philosophy?
readingList.notes: A canonical work on the conception of philosophy as a choice of life (bios) rather than doctrinal discourse.

readingList.author: Pierre Hadot
readingList.title: Spiritual Exercises and Ancient Philosophy
readingList.notes: The articulation between dialectical askesis, epimeleia heautou, and the transformation of the cosmic and moral gaze.

readingList.author: Plato
readingList.title: Republic, Book I (Classical Greek reading and translation seminar)
readingList.notes: A close analysis of the dialogue with Cephalus, Polemarchus, and Thrasymachus's violent aporetic intrusion.
